Header:
Date: 2025-11-12
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~67 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (VectorScale), Tom Delgado (VectorScale SRE), Aisha Khan (VectorScale ML Eng)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive to walk through GPU runtime profiling results, discuss kernel selection heuristics, compare TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) vs vLLM behavior, and look at CUDA graphs and KV cache interactions. Team wants to validate pilot performance and surface next steps for an enterprise pilot in a VPC/on-prem setup.

Topics:
- Kernel selection and where Redwood picks cuDNN/TensorRT paths
- vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM throughput/latency tradeoffs
- CUDA graphs warmup and memory pinning effects
- KV cache and batching strategies impact on p99 latency
- Quantization profiles and accuracy regressions
- VPC/on-prem constraints for driver/kernel availability

Action items and next steps captured at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run about an hour. Marcus and I will start with the profiling summary, then hand it off.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Great, thanks. We're most interested in the kernel selection part \u2014 our perf engineer said some weird kernels were chosen for 8k context.
[00:20] Marcus Chen: Yeah, so quick context \u2014 we profiled your 7B/13B family on p4d (A100) and an A40 node to compare TensorRT-LLM path vs a vllm-optimized runtime. We captured nvprof/ptx traces plus cudagraphs runtime.
[00:35] Tom Delgado: Quick question, when you say "vllm" do you mean the open-source runtime or the more customized vLLM infra you mentioned in the deck?
[00:42] Marcus Chen: Right, sorry. I mean the open-source vLLM binary with Redwood's continuous batching layer on top; sometimes notes show it as vllm or v-L-L-M in the logs.
[00:52] Aisha Khan: We also have quantized weights using 4-bit Q4 and an experimental 5-bit recipe \u2014 curious how that interacts with TensorRT.
[01:00] Marcus Chen: Good point. TensorRT-LLM supports INT8/FP16 flows and some 4-bit pipelines via custom plugins, but there's often kernel fallback in two places: first, the matmul path if the kernel isn't available for your shape, second, attention kernels for causal masks.
[01:18] Lena Park: I'll share the profiling deck \u2014 link in notes: https://redwood.team/profiling/vector-scale/profiling-deck.pdf
[01:24] Priya Nair: Thanks. Can you talk through kernel selection heuristics? At what point does Redwood prefer TensorRT kernels vs cuBLAS/cutlass?
[01:33] Marcus Chen: Sure \u2014 short answer: heuristic is based on model architecture shape, sequence length distribution, batch size, and whether KV cache is warm. For shorter sequences and high QPS with small batches, Redwood tends to favor persistent cuBLAS/cutlass fused kernels; for long sequences and large matmuls TensorRT LLM kernels often win due to fused attention and faster softmax/scale math. But there are shape corners where fallback to generic kernels happens \u2014 e.g., odd hidden sizes or unsupported quant layouts.
[02:04] Tom Delgado: We saw a spike in p95 latency when switching from batch size 1 to 4 with KV cache on. Is that a batching artifact?
[02:12] Marcus Chen: Likely. Batching interacts badly with KV cache locality \u2014 if you batch requests with very different prompt prefixes, you can't reuse the prefix KV efficiently, so you pay both in memory and compute. We showed an experiment in the deck where enabling workload-aware batching reduced cost but increased p99 by ~10-20% for mixed-length traffic.
[02:37] Aisha Khan: And how do CUDA graphs come into play? We tried enabling graphs but saw higher memory spikes.
[02:44] Marcus Chen: CUDA graphs help by eliminating launch overheads, but they require deterministic execution and pinned memory. If your kernel selection changes (fallbacks), the captured graph can become invalid and cause replays or full re-capture, which leads to transient memory growth. Also, cudagraphs combined with dynamic KV cache sizes need careful graph partitioning \u2014 you can't capture all lengths in one graph without a lot of memory.
[03:08] Priya Nair: So for on-prem VPC deployments, we have older drivers (470.x) for compatibility. Will that affect TensorRT kernel availability?
[03:17] Marcus Chen: Yes \u2014 TensorRT and some optimized plugins require newer cuda/cuDNN/TensorRT stacks. On older driver stacks you'll see more kernel fallbacks. For private deployments we recommend a minimum driver set (CUDA 11.8 / cuDNN 8.4 / TensorRT 8.x) \u2014 we'll put the exact matrix in the security + infra doc.
[03:32] Tom Delgado: Any gotchas for KMS or encryption that affect performance?
[03:36] Lena Park: Short answer: KMS calls are async to the runtime; they shouldn't be on the hot path for token generation. But HSM-backed keys can add latency on startup or key rotation events if not cached. We'll include our KMS best practices for pilot.
[03:50] Marcus Chen: Back to perf \u2014 we instrumented kernel-level time and saw that on p4d TensorRT-LLM gained 1.6x throughput for long sequences vs vLLM, but with a slightly higher tail latency when KV cache misses occurred. vLLM showed more consistent p99 but lower peak throughput on A40.
[04:12] Aisha Khan: That matches our internal runs. Did you isolate whether the p99 is from attention kernel or from memory allocs?
[04:18] Marcus Chen: Mostly attention + occasional cuMemAlloc spikes when designers don't pre-reserve KV buffers. We recommend preallocating a small pool and using a circular buffer for KV to avoid per-request allocs. Also use the runtime setting to pin host memory for cudagraph captures.
[04:38] Priya Nair: You mentioned quantization regressions earlier \u2014 can you elaborate? We saw subtle semantic differences with 5-bit.
[04:45] Marcus Chen: Yeah, smaller-bit quantization often changes softmax sharpness and can amplify system-level beam differences. Our eval harness runs the customer's eval prompts (we ask for a 200 prompt holdout) and runs quality regressions. If 5-bit causes >X% drop on rouge/bertscore we flag it. For pilot we typically recommend Q4 + Bias correction for safety.
[05:05] Tom Delgado: For the pilot run, we want to compare a real traffic replay with KV cache warm vs cold start. How do you suggest we run it?
[05:12] Marcus Chen: Two runs: 1) warm-cache steady-state replay with same session IDs to reuse KV; 2) cold-start mix with 10% long sequences to stress cudagraph re-captures. We'll provide a script that replays traffic with session affinity.
[05:26] Lena Park: We'll also attach the kernel selection logs \u2014 small snippet example in the deck.
[05:31] Priya Nair: Artifact links?
[05:33] Lena Park: Yes: profiling deck (above), sample kernel logs: https://redwood.team/profiling/vector-scale/kernel-logs.txt, cudagraph traces: https://redwood.team/profiling/vector-scale/cudagraphs.tar.gz
[05:45] Aisha Khan: Nice. Are there any quick config knobs we can flip to reduce p99 now?
[05:50] Marcus Chen: A few: reduce max batch delay to favor latency, enable prefix policing to avoid mixing long vs short prompts in the same batch, enable preallocated KV pools, and disable graph capture for very dynamic workloads. Also try hybrid kernels: force cuBLAS for matmul and TensorRT for attention in mixed-mode if your stack supports it.
[06:11] Tom Delgado: How invasive is hybrid kernel mode? Does it require rebuilds?
[06:14] Marcus Chen: No rebuilds; it's a runtime config in Redwood that toggles kernel preference. It can be applied per-model. We'll show the flag in the runbook.
[06:23] Priya Nair: About VPC/on-prem again: if we can't upgrade drivers, can we still run a Redwood private agent?
[06:30] Lena Park: Yes, you can run a private agent but expect reduced perf due to fallbacks. We'll recommend a minimum hardware/driver profile in the infra worksheet. For true parity with hosted, we recommend matching our validated stack.
[06:41] Marcus Chen: One more observation \u2014 for prompt lengths beyond ~4k, we start seeing different kernel shapes chosen; memory-bound fused attention kernels can be better but require larger workspace, which hurts consolidation on dense multi-tenant nodes. Tradeoff there for Dedicated pools.
[06:58] Priya Nair: That helps. Can we get the exact command lines you ran for nvprof/cupti so our infra team can reproduce?
[07:05] Marcus Chen: Absolutely \u2014 will include in the runbook. We'll also include the script to collect per-kernel timings and the mapping to Redwood's kernel names.
[07:12] Lena Park: OK let's do a quick recap and actions. Marcus, you want to recap the tech notes?
[07:16] Marcus Chen: Sure \u2014 Recap: 1) TRT-LLM wins on long-seq throughput but can have higher tail on KV misses; 2) vLLM gives more stable p99 but lower throughput; 3) cudagraphs reduce launch overhead but need pinned memory and stable kernel selection; 4) quantization needs eval holdouts; 5) for on-prem, match validated driver/TensorRT stack or expect fallbacks.
[07:38] Priya Nair: Sounds good. We'll provision the sample traffic and try the weekend benchmark.
[07:43] Tom Delgado: And we'll try the hybrid kernel flags first to see tail impact.
[07:47] Lena Park: Great. I'll send the profiling deck, kernel logs, and runbook. Marcus will send the cudagraph capture script. We'll schedule follow-up week of 11/24.
[07:55] Aisha Khan: Thanks everyone, useful session.
[07:58] Lena Park: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifact links and action items.

End of call.
